facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: Shiva's immediate answer was to explode a tremendous burst of power from his third eye, which created a horrendous, emaciated, ravenous lion.
facts.source_name: Skanda Purana, Kartika Masa Mahatmya, Chapter 17
facts.text: In the Skanda Purana, the demon king Jalandhara challenges Lord Shiva by sending the emissary Rahu to demand Goddess Parvati, which causes an enraged Shiva to unleash a ravenous, lion-faced entity from between his eyebrows.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: So Kirtimukha willingly ate his body starting with its tail as per Lord Shiva's order, stopping only when his face remained.
facts.source_name: Skanda Purana, Kartika Masa Mahatmya, Chapter 17
facts.text: According to the Skanda Purana, when Rahu begged for mercy and was spared, the starving creature obeyed Shiva's command to appease its hunger by devouring its own body until only its face remained.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: Shiva, who was pleased with the result, gave it the name 'glorious face', and declared that it should always be at the door of his temples.
facts.source_name: Skanda Purana, Kartika Masa Mahatmya, Chapter 17
facts.text: The Skanda Purana states that Shiva was so pleased by the creature's unhesitating obedience that he named it Kirtimukha, or 'Face of Glory', and ordained that no one would gain the merit of temple worship without first honoring it at the entrance.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: The kirtimukha is essentially an ornamental motif in art, which has its origin in a legend from the Skanda Purana and the Shiva Purana.
facts.source_name: Shiva Purana, Rudra Samhita, Yuddha Khanda
facts.text: The Rudra Samhita of the Shiva Purana similarly recounts the creation of a terrifying being from Shiva's wrath during his confrontation with the envoys of Jalandhara.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: The 'Kirtimukha' is the crown or crest jewel in the architectural features like arches, Gavaksas, lintels, etc.
facts.source_name: Mayamata: Treatise on Housing Architecture and Iconography
facts.text: Classical Sanskrit architectural treatises such as the Mayamata mandate the carving of Kirtimukha at the apex of doorway arches (torana) and deity frames (prabhavali) as an auspicious crest.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The lintel seems to have been ornamented by the models of the chaitya window of the early Gupta style, each containing a Kirtimukha.
facts.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India Memoir No. 4
facts.text: Excavations by the Archaeological Survey of India at Nagari in Rajasthan unearthed early Gupta-period temple doorway lintel fragments bearing carved chaitya windows that each contained a Kirtimukha head.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The kudu, or apex of a candrasala, at Ajanta Caves 19 and 26 is, to my knowledge... Kirtimukha with lion-face (Ajanta).
facts.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Ajanta Cave Documentation
facts.text: Surveys conducted by the Archaeological Survey of India at the Ajanta Caves revealed 5th-century CE rock-cut candrasala arches in Cave 19 and Cave 26 that feature sculpted Kirtimukha masks at their crests.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The central ratha has a large panel on each side, called chandrashaala, which has a circular centre, gana-s on either side, and a kirtimukha pouring out pearls from the top.
facts.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India Western Circle Report
facts.text: Archaeological Survey of India documentation of the 5th-century CE Gupta temple at Bhumara confirmed the use of stone chandrashala medallions framed by Kirtimukhas spewing garlands of pearls.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: terracotta tiles showing swastika and kirtimukha, Dharmachakra, Votive Stupas in pipal leaf motiff and sample of charred rice are some note worthy objects in this gallery.
facts.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India Nalanda Museum Catalogue
facts.text: Excavations at the ancient Nalanda Mahavihara in Bihar conducted by the Archaeological Survey of India uncovered molded terracotta tiles depicting Kirtimukha visages alongside early Buddhist motifs such as the Dharmachakra and Swastika.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Kirtimukha at Kasivisvesvara Temple at Lakkundi, Gadag district, Karnataka, India.
facts.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India Lakkundi Survey
facts.text: Surveys by the Archaeological Survey of India at the 11th-century CE Kasivisvesvara Temple at Lakkundi in Karnataka documented elaborately carved Kirtimukhas surmounting tower niches and doorways.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: This is succeeded by a kirtimukha, and then by... The octagonal section is divided into four bands, with the uppermost band containing a depiction of kirtimukha.
facts.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India Modhera Survey
facts.text: At the 11th-century CE Sun Temple at Modhera in Gujarat, preserved by the Archaeological Survey of India, architectural analysis confirmed that multiple pillar tiers in the assembly hall are decorated with carved Kirtimukha friezes.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: it has been suggested that the origin of the kirtimukha may be found in the Chinese T'ao Tien, the 'devourer' and in the lion masks from classical times.
facts.source_name: Myths and Symbols in Indian Art and Civilization by Heinrich Zimmer
facts.text: Art historians debate whether the Kirtimukha developed independently from indigenous Vedic solar lion iconography (Simhamukha) or was influenced through ancient cultural transmission by Hellenistic Gorgon masks and Chinese Taotie motifs.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: This face is sometimes confused with another sculptural element, the lion face (Simhamukha). However, in order to be a Kirtimukha it has to be engaged in swallowing, for the Kirtimukha is the figure of the 'all consuming'.
facts.source_name: The Hindu Temple by Stella Kramrisch
facts.text: Scholars disagree over whether the jawless Kirtimukha constitutes an entirely separate symbolic entity from the full-jawed Simhamukha or if both terms merely describe regional stylistic variations of the same protective mask.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: Home version, Sold as a nazar battu for the main door.
facts.source_name: Popular Folklore Traditions of Western and Southern India
facts.text: In widespread regional Indian folklore, hanging a brass or terracotta Kirtimukha mask directly over the main doorway of a residence functions as a protective talisman (nazar battu) to swallow ill will and the evil eye.

intro.prompt: 9:16 vertical, 1080x1920, about 8 seconds, photorealistic and cinematic, bright vivid colour. Setting: dramatic close view of a huge carved stone lion face with bulging eyes, sharp fangs and no lower jaw, crowning an ancient Indian temple doorway, storm clouds and lightning behind, oil lamps flickering below, wet stone glistening, deep shadows, filling the frame. The background is real and in motion behind him (as fits the place: waves, mist, leaves, flags, lamps flickering, people walking, traffic, light shifting); never a still, flat or heavily blurred backdrop. If the scene shows the past, it is ancient India: Indian people in dhotis, sarees and angavastram, warriors with bows, spears and bronze or leather armour, carved stone pillars, oil lamps; never European knights, plate armour, castles or anything medieval European. Framing: medium shot from the waist up, his whole head and both shoulders inside the frame with clear space above his hair and on both sides, and he stays framed like this to the end; do not crop the top of his head. Lighting: warm key light on the face, a soft rim light on the hair, matched to the scene; flattering, no harsh shadows, no dull or flat grey look. SG [locked] standing relaxed and upright, shoulders open, wearing a mustard kurta. Speaks from the first frame, mouth matched to the words, steady eye contact with the lens. Face and delivery: a confident, charismatic documentary presenter. Calm, natural face with a pleasant, warm smile, relaxed eyebrows, eyes soft and focused on the viewer. On "sharir kyun kha gaya" the eyes narrow a little with intrigue and the head tilts slightly, as if sharing a secret. On "Suniye, twist yahan hai!" a warm, confident smile and one small nod. Natural blinking, subtle head movement. No exaggerated expressions: no wide eyes, no raised eyebrows, no open-mouth surprise, no big grin, no frown; never sad, gloomy, worried or tired. Voice: warm, clear, measured, with quiet intensity; a short pause before "sharir kyun kha gaya". Hands: one slow, small gesture toward the scene behind him on the first line, then hands rest; no fast or large arm movements. Camera: eye level, a very slight slow push-in, slight handheld feel. Empty hands, no prop. @SGMythWorld watermark in the top right corner, white, bold, 80% opacity. No captions, no subtitles, no other on-screen text. No hologram, no floating screen, no graph, no chart, no laptop, tablet, monitor, TV or glowing blue panel anywhere in the frame. Export at 1080x1920.
